The cited evidence indicates that decisional algorithms cannot replace global introspection (GI) in the individual causality assessment of spontaneously reported adverse drug reactions, because in a comparison against an expert panel's WHO GI assessment the algorithms achieved high sensitivity (average 93%, positive predictive value 89%) but very low specificity (average 7%, negative predictive value 31%).

In that study, an expert panel assessed causality of 500 adverse reports by using the WHO global introspection (GI) method, the same reports were independently assessed using 15 published algorithms, and the causality assessment level 'possible' was considered the lower limit for a report to be considered drug related.

Sensitivity was determined by the proportion of reports simultaneously classified as drug related by a given algorithm and the GI method, whereas specificity was measured as the proportion of reports simultaneously considered non-drug related; the reported average specificity of 7% and negative predictive value of 31% mean that the algorithms frequently classified reports as drug related when the GI method did not, so the cited results do not support replacing GI with decisional algorithms.

Specialty pharmaceuticals have evolved beyond their status as niche drugs designed to treat rare conditions and are now poised to become the standard of care in a wide variety of common chronic illnesses.

The promise of specialty pharmaceuticals described in the source is increased life expectancy, improved quality of life, enhanced workplace productivity, decreased burden of disease, and reduced health care spending, all of which comes at a significant cost.

The cited source provides no definitive determination of whether specialty pharmaceuticals are worth their price; it reports that determining the value of these medications is hampered by a lack of robust pharmacoeconomic data.
Due in part to the cost of these therapies, payers are increasingly demanding evidence of their value.

With the specialty pharmaceutical pipeline overflowing with new medicines and an aging population increasingly relying on these novel treatments to treat common diseases, the challenge of managing the costs associated with these agents can be daunting.
Aided by sophisticated pharmacoeconomic models to assess value, the cost impacts of these specialty drugs can be appropriately controlled.

The cited evidence is insufficient to establish that vaginal intraepithelial neoplasia (VAIN) has the same evolution/natural history as cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN): the study set out to ascertain whether vaginal lesions have a natural history similar to cervical lesions but reported only cross-sectional comparisons of synchronous vaginal and cervical lesions in a retrospective biopsy-identified series, not progression or regression over time.

In a retrospective study that identified patients with vaginal lesions and synchronous cervical lesions through biopsy, patients with mild vaginal lesions (warts and koilocytosis, and low-grade VAIN) had mild cervical lesions (koilocytosis, warts, CIN I with and without koilocytosis) significantly more frequently than severe cervical lesions (CIN II and III, cervical carcinoma).

Using koilocytosis as a marker, the rate of "active" cervical lesions in patients with "active" vaginal lesions was significantly higher than the rate of "non active" cervical lesions in those patients.
The differences in rates of mild cervical lesions and severe cervical lesions among patients with high-grade VAIN and low-grade VAIN (with and without koilocytosis) were not significant.

Because the reported design compared synchronous vaginal and cervical lesions cross-sectionally rather than following lesions over time, these findings cannot establish whether VAIN and CIN share the same evolution, such as comparable rates of progression or regression.

The occurrence of cerebro-mediastinal tuberculosis in an immuno-competent child had not been previously described to the authors' knowledge, and the reported case was a seven-year-old girl who presented with an infantile encephalopathy dating from birth and a history of recurrent infections.

In that seven-year-old girl, spinal and cerebral MRI showed a mediastinal mass involving the spine and cerebral lesions evocative of tuberculomas, the tuberculin interdermal reaction was positive, and culture of a vertebral biopsy was positive for Koch bacillus.
Anti-tuberculosis treatment improved the child's general and local status, and an extensive immunological work-up was normal.

The child described has a probable Say-Barber-Miller syndrome, with a history of infantile encephalopathy since birth characterized by facial dysmorphy evocative of a bird face, microcephaly, mental retardation, and recurrent infections.

The report states that the authors discuss a putative causative link between this syndrome and the occurrence of tuberculosis, i.e., the association is presented as a hypothesis for discussion rather than as an established causal relationship.

Because the cited evidence is a single case description in which the syndrome and the tuberculosis occurred in the same child and the causal relationship is described only as putative, it cannot establish that probable Say-Barber-Miller syndrome causes cerebro-mediastinal tuberculosis.

Yes — in guinea pig cochlear histology, halofantrine produced dose-related inner-ear damage, with hair-cell loss and distortion and spiral ganglion cell loss in both the therapeutic dose and double therapeutic dose groups.

Thirty guinea pigs were divided into three groups — a control group, a halofantrine therapeutic dose group and a halofantrine double therapeutic dose group — and one cochlea specimen from each animal was stained with haematoxylin and eosin while the other was stained with toluidine blue.
No changes were detected in the control group.
The halofantrine therapeutic dose group showed loss and distortion of inner hair cells and inner phalangeal cells, and loss of spiral ganglia cells.
In the halofantrine double therapeutic dose group, the inner and outer hair cells were distorted and there was loss of spiral ganglia cells.

This evidence is limited to animal cochlear histopathology: the report states there have been no studies investigating halofantrine's effect on hearing and that studies on adverse reactions in humans are insufficient, so these guinea pig findings cannot establish ototoxicity or hearing outcomes in humans.
